Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to hold talks with United States special envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders in Norway, aimed at ending the war with Russia.
The prime ministers of Norway and Finland will attend the talks in Oslo on Tuesday, while President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is expected to attend remotely because of illness.

The meeting comes as Trump continues to publicly castigate Zelenskyy, accusing him of not wanting to end the war and suggesting that someone else should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Zelenskyy requested that Witkoff and Kushner participate in Tuesday’s discussions.
In a post on X before the talks, Zelenskyy said he had engaged in a “substantive conversation” with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about missile interceptors, intelligence sharing and Starlink, a satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Last week, Zelenskyy accused Washington of withholding intelligence from Kyiv and limiting Starlink’s internet speed. Ukraine’s armed forces use SpaceX’s military-grade internet network Starshield for several operations, including drone attacks.
Zelenskyy did not confirm whether Rubio had committed to addressing the issues raised, including supplying Ukraine with crucial US-made Patriot missile interceptors and restoring intelligence sharing and Starshield services. However, he described the discussion as “constructive” and said the two had agreed to speak again soon.
The talks come as the two warring sides continue to launch long-range air attacks on each other.
At least three people were killed across Ukraine in Russian attacks on Tuesday. A Russian drone struck a highway connecting Kyiv to the Black Sea port of Odesa, killing three people and injuring four, Kyiv’s regional prosecutor’s office confirmed.
Meanwhile, more than 32,000 families are without electricity after Ukraine’s largest private energy company, DTEK, confirmed that three of its energy facilities in the southern Odesa region had been hit by Russia.
The governor of Russia’s Tambov Oblast said on Tuesday that a fire had broken out at an oil pumping station after an overnight Ukrainian drone attack. Yevgeny Pervyshov said four drones were intercepted.
Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, while easing pressure on Russia, including lifting sanctions on its diesel exports. Trump has been eager to bring down energy prices, which have surged as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Zelenskyy has described the agreement to waive sanctions on Russian diesel as a “reward” for President Vladimir Putin, warning that it would only embolden him.

items.title: The Federal Reserve Just Warned More Rate Hikes Are Likely Coming. History Has Good and Bad News for Investors - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Federal Reserve Just Warned More Rate Hikes Are Likely Coming. History Has Good and Bad News for Investors  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The S&P 500 has roared higher over more than three years, extending a bull market, with investors piling into artificial intelligence (AI) stocks and other growth players. The famous benchmark is heading for an increase of about 100% since the start of 2023. Investors have been eager to get in on the next big thing in technology, and in recent years, the generally positive economic backdrop has buoyed demand for growth-oriented stocks.
But in more recent times, one stubborn problem has knocked on the door: rising inflation. Turmoil in Iran has led to surging energy prices, and that's weighed on households and the corporate world. The Federal Reserve stepped in last month, doing something for the first time in three years. Policymakers lifted the benchmark interest rate, the federal funds rate, by a quarter point to the range of 3.75% to 4%.
And the Fed just warned that more rate hikes are likely coming. Against this backdrop, history has good and bad news for investors.
First, though, let's start with a summary of the market situation over the past few years. As mentioned, the S&P 500 has climbed amid excitement over AI and demand for growth stocks in general. The economic environment in the early days of this movement was supportive, but progressively, inflationary pressures emerged and worsened amid soaring oil prices this year.
Even with this headwind present, the S&P 500 has advanced, reaching multiple record highs. AI stocks have faced more difficult trading days than they did in the past, but they still have climbed, many in the double and triple digits.
The Fed, in a move to tame inflation, last month lifted rates and, in the Federal Open Market Committee meeting minutes, warned that more rate hikes are likely coming.
"With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the policymakers wrote. The Fed also emphasized its commitment to pursuing its dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability.
Meanwhile, the probability of a rate hike during the Fed's December meeting has reached more than 88%, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Though expectations are for no change at the policymakers' next meeting at the end of this month, all of the above support the idea of another rate increase just beyond that point.
Now let's consider the bad and good news for investors. The bad news is that higher interest rate levels generally aren't positive for the stock market. For a couple of reasons. First, higher rates may be a drag on corporate earnings, as they represent greater borrowing costs for companies and pressure on revenue for companies heavily depending on consumer spending. During times of higher rates, consumers' wallets feel the pressure as they face higher rates on credit cards and student loans, for example. And they generally favor spending on essentials over discretionary purchases. This may equal lower revenue for certain companies. Also, during periods of higher interest rates, some investors prefer bonds, as they offer higher yields and are seen as less risky than stocks.
And all of this may translate into weaker performance for the stock market. Anticipating this, certain investors may hesitate to buy stocks, compounding the problem.
Now, here's the good news. History shows us that, though the S&P 500 may fall in anticipation of and during times of higher rates, these tough times aren't long-lasting.
As the chart above shows, the index has always recovered and gone on to gain significantly in the years to follow.
So what does this mean for you as an investor? Periods of higher interest rates are buying opportunities . At these moments, you may find many quality stocks trading at very reasonable valuations, so it is the moment to pick them up at a bargain and hold on. History has demonstrated over and over that this move may offer you spectacular results over the long run.

December Brent crude trades at $111.36 a barrel as Iran says two oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz
By Cris Tolomia · 2 min read · Updated October 20, 2026
West Texas Intermediate crude futures for November delivery rose 5.23% to $109.08 a barrel as of 7:04 a.m. ET on Tuesday as attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz escalated. The contract expires on Tuesday.
WTI is poised for a ninth straight winning session and a gain of nearly 20% for the month. December Brent crude futures climbed 1.65% to $111.36 a barrel, a peak not seen since May, according to CNBC .
No fewer than 18 vessels have been targeted in the strait during the last fortnight, according to CNBC. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Tuesday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers caught fire after striking mines its naval unit had planted, according to CNBC.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran's reply to any U.S. strike would come "in equal measure, if not more forcefully," according to CNBC. President Donald Trump said this month that the U.S. military will hold off on striking Iran until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to CNBC.
Tamas Varga, an analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told CNBC that the firmness of front-end WTI as its contract nears expiry signals a squeeze on worldwide oil supply. "It is a reflection of falling export volumes from the Middle East as tanker attacks and Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure intensify," he said.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said shipments of crude leaving the Gulf have rebounded to nearly 80% of what they were before the war, according to Euronews . Supplies of refined fuels are more limited, according to Euronews.
Oil prices surged at the start of September after U.S. military action against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz , which followed Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway. The U.S. and Iran had signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, but the agreement collapsed. Iran has since demanded sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. naval blockade before the waterway can reopen.
The International Energy Agency cut its 2026 global oil supply forecast to 102 million barrels per day in August, citing the breakdown of the ceasefire and a renewed closure of the strait.

Image caption, Monfils and Svitolina played in the mixed doubles together at this year's US Open and reached the semi-finals
Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player GaÃ«l Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.
The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".
"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.
She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".
"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.
It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.
"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.
Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."
The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.
Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".
Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.
However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.
Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.
Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

items.summary: European Chip Stocks Fall More Than 4% as AI Investment Concerns Trigger Asian Sell-Off  Yahoo Finance UK
items.content:
European Chip Stocks Fall More Than 4% as AI Investment Concerns Trigger Asian Sell-Off
Semiconductor ©Adobe Stock Images European semiconductor stocks declined sharply on Tuesday, following losses across Asian technology markets as investors reassessed the financial sustainability of spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Shares in several major European chipmakers and semiconductor equipment suppliers fell more than 3% during early trading, extending the volatility seen across global technology markets.
Technoprobe (BIT:TPRO), Siltronic (TG:WAF) and Soitec (EU:SOI) each declined more than 4%.
ASM International (EU:ASM), BE Semiconductor (EU:BESI), Aixtron (TG:AIXA), STMicroelectronics (BIT:STMMI) and Infineon (TG:IFX) all recorded losses exceeding 3% by 07:34 GMT.
The declines followed renewed concerns about the scale of investment in artificial intelligence and whether companies involved in the sector can generate sufficient returns to justify their spending.
South Korean Semiconductor Shares Lead Asian Declines
The weakness in Europe followed a substantial sell-off among South Korean semiconductor manufacturers.
Samsung Electronics (USOTC:SSNHZ) closed 3% lower, while memory chip producer SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) declined 4.2%.
South Korea's benchmark Kospi index fell 3.7% to 5,552.74 points, ending two consecutive sessions of gains.
The index recorded its lowest closing level since 7 April, reflecting broader selling pressure across the country's equity market.
The latest declines reversed part of the recovery in Asian semiconductor shares during the previous two sessions.
Investor concerns remain focused on the financing requirements and profitability of AI-related investment, particularly as technology companies commit substantial capital to infrastructure development.
Wall Street Technology Recovery Fails to Support European Shares
The European sell-off contrasted with Monday's performance on Wall Street, where major US technology stocks recovered some of their recent losses.
The S&P 500 advanced 0.4%, following its weakest weekly performance since June.
The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.1%, supported by its substantial exposure to technology and artificial intelligence-related companies.
However, the recovery was concentrated in technology stocks, while most US shares outside the sector declined.
This divergence suggests that investor sentiment towards AI-related equities remains uneven across markets, with gains in selected US technology companies failing to prevent further losses among Asian and European semiconductor manufacturers.
French Political Unrest Adds Pressure to European Markets
European equities also faced broader selling pressure linked to political and civil unrest in France.
Major European stock indices declined more than 1% as violent demonstrations raised uncertainty about the French government's fiscal response.
Concerns that additional public spending could be required to address public dissatisfaction contributed to pressure on sovereign bond markets.
Government bond yields increased, adding to the financial market uncertainty affecting European equities.
For semiconductor investors, the combination of sector-specific concerns about AI investment returns and broader financial market volatility has created a challenging trading environment.
The declines across European chipmakers indicate that investors are reassessing valuations and financial expectations throughout the semiconductor supply chain.
However, the reported share price movements do not establish any immediate deterioration in the companies' underlying operating performance.
Investors will be monitoring developments in Asian semiconductor markets, the performance of US technology shares and further indications of whether AI-related capital spending can support sustainable profitability.
European bond market conditions and political developments in France may also continue to influence broader market sentiment.

Gold eases as oil-driven inflation worries weigh on sentiment
Gold inched higher on Tuesday, helped by a softer U.S. dollar, as market participants looked ahead to next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting for clues on the future path of interest rates.
Gold eased on Tuesday as firmer oil prices ​fueled inflation concerns, while ​investors awaited next week's ​Federal Reserve meeting for further direction on U.S. interest rates.
Spot gold fell 0.51% to $4,118.76 an ounce, while U.S. gold futures for December delivery dropped ⁠0.55% ‌to $4,137.20 an ounce.
"Oil is over $100, so I ⁠think basically the story this morning is just a stronger, higher-priced oil is putting pressure on precious metals," said Bob Haberkorn, senior market strategist at StoneX.
Oil prices advanced on Tuesday, with ‌Brent hovering around a five-month high as traders priced in geopolitical risks from Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks ​in the Gulf.
Gold is still down around 26.4% from its record high of $5,594.82 in January and roughly 22% from levels at the start of the Iran war, when concerns over energy ⁠inflation reinforced bets on interest rate hikes.
The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter point ‌in September, its first hike this year.
While recent comments ‌from Fed officials signaling little urgency for further policy tightening have tempered expectations of a rate hike at the central bank's October 27-28 policy meeting, traders see a ⁠92% chance of a hike in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Gold is ⁠traditionally seen as an inflation hedge, but it loses its ⁠appeal as a non-yielding asset in a high-interest-rate environment.
Investors are also watching next week's U.S. Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data, the Federal ​Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, for clues ‌on whether inflation pressures remain persistent and how that could shape the rate outlook.
Elsewhere in Japan, central bank Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation was "quite close" to the 2% target, signaling scope for further rate hikes.
Among other metals, spot silver was steady at $57.08 per ​ounce, platinum fell 0.29% lower ‌to $1,635.48 per ounce and palladium dropped 1.54% to $1,102.45 per ounce.

Large gold nugget ©James St. John Gold prices declined for a third consecutive session on Tuesday as elevated oil prices raised concerns about persistent US inflation and the possibility that the Federal Reserve could maintain higher interest rates for longer.
Spot gold fell 0.4% to $4,123.32 per ounce by 04:46 ET (08:46 GMT), while gold futures declined 0.5% to $4,141.09 an ounce.
The precious metal had already lost 0.6% in Monday's session, following a weekly decline, as investors reassessed the outlook for US monetary policy.
Gold prices extended their decline to a third session, with spot bullion trading at $4,123.32 per ounce.
Brent crude remained above $110 a barrel, increasing concerns about energy-driven inflation.
Markets assigned an 83% probability to the Federal Reserve leaving rates unchanged at its October 27–28 meeting.
CME FedWatch indicated a 94% probability of a December rate increase, according to the reported market pricing.
Upcoming US inflation data could influence expectations for monetary policy, although the PCE report will follow the October Fed decision.
The latest decline reflects changing expectations for US interest rates as investors assess the inflationary consequences of rising energy costs.
Gold does not generate interest income, making it sensitive to changes in bond yields and monetary policy expectations.
When investors anticipate higher interest rates, interest-bearing assets can become relatively more attractive than bullion.
The relationship is particularly relevant ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting, when policymakers will assess whether inflationary pressures justify maintaining restrictive financial conditions.
The latest selling also follows a period of weakness in gold prices, indicating that concerns about interest rates are continuing to influence trading sentiment.
Brent crude traded above $110 a barrel on Tuesday, remaining near its highest level in approximately five months.
Oil prices have been supported by concerns about possible disruptions to energy shipments through the Persian Gulf following reported attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement also claimed on Monday that it had carried out attacks against Saudi Arabian energy, airport and military infrastructure, including an Aramco facility.
The reported developments have increased uncertainty about regional energy supplies.
Higher crude prices can affect inflation through transportation, fuel and production costs, potentially increasing expenses for businesses and consumers.
For gold investors, the significance lies in how persistent energy inflation could influence the Federal Reserve's future interest rate decisions.
Although geopolitical uncertainty can sometimes support demand for gold, the latest price movements suggest that monetary policy concerns are currently exerting downward pressure.
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet on October 27–28, with market participants largely anticipating no change in interest rates.
According to the CME FedWatch probabilities cited in the report, traders assigned an 83% likelihood to rates remaining unchanged at the upcoming meeting.
The same market pricing indicated a 94% probability of an interest rate increase in December.
These probabilities represent market expectations rather than confirmed policy decisions and may change as new economic information becomes available.
In September, the Fed increased its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years, citing the need to address inflationary pressures.
The central bank's next decision will therefore be closely watched for indications of how policymakers are balancing inflation risks against broader economic conditions.
For bullion markets, any change in expectations about the timing or direction of interest rates could influence demand.
Recent US consumer price figures showed inflation rising more than economists had anticipated, largely because of higher gasoline and diesel prices.
The increase reinforced concerns that energy costs could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring inflation back towards its 2% target.
Investors are now awaiting the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, one of the Fed's preferred measures of inflation.
The report is scheduled for release later this month, after the central bank's October policy announcement.
Consequently, the upcoming Fed decision will take place without the benefit of the latest PCE figures.
The data may nevertheless influence expectations for subsequent policy meetings, particularly if it indicates that inflationary pressures are proving persistent.
The immediate focus for gold markets is the Federal Reserve's October 27–28 meeting and any guidance concerning the future path of US interest rates.
Developments in crude oil prices and shipping conditions around the Strait of Hormuz will also remain relevant because of their potential effects on inflation.
After the Fed meeting, the upcoming PCE inflation report will provide another opportunity to assess whether US price pressures are moderating.
For investors following precious metals, the interaction between inflation, interest rate expectations and geopolitical uncertainty remains central to gold's near-term trading environment.

items.title: Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
items.summary: Reliance is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers and contain oil prices amid the war on Iran.
items.content:
Share Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest on social media
A security guard stands at the gate of Essar Oil's refinery on the outskirts of the Jamnagar in the western Indian state of Gujarat February 1, 2007 [Reuters]
New Delhi, India — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in India for a two-day visit, during which he is set to tour the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, a major player in global oil markets.
Reliance’s crude refinery in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state is the world’s largest single-site refinery. In many ways, Reliance Industries’ businesses sit at the crossroads of the ongoing global energy crisis.
The conglomerate is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers, while also trying to contain oil prices amid the war on Iran, on top of rising diesel costs in the US, where a crucial midterm election looms. Reliance has also only recently committed to a major investment in the US, which President Donald Trump’s administration has cited as an example of its successes in luring global capital.
Rubio is skipping the capital, New Delhi, at a time when the US-India bilateral relationship has been rocky, strained by a string of friction points — and an elusive trade deal.
So why is the top US diplomat visiting the world’s largest single-site oil refinery?
Secretary of State Marco Rubio shakes hands with US Consul-General in Mumbai Yuriy Fedkiw as he disembarks from a plane after arriving at Mumbai airport in India, October 20, 2026 [Kylie Cooper/Reuters] Where is Rubio visiting?
After meetings in Mumbai, India’s financial hub in the western state of Maharashtra, Rubio will fly to Jamnagar in neighbouring Gujarat, near the Gulf of Kutch. Jamnagar opens into the Arabian Sea and is home to Reliance Industries’ refining complex, a major hub for crude processing and fuel exports, which processes 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd).
Rubio had visited India earlier this year too, but this trip “is a little more business-focused”, the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, told reporters last week. A readout from Rubio’s office noted that he would “meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation”.
“[At Jamnagar] he will meet some of the folks at Reliance,” Gor said.
The Reliance Industries oil refinery in Jamnagar, Gujarat, India, on July 31, 2021 [Bloomberg] What’s in Jamnagar?
The world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex has a combined crude-processing capacity of 1.4 million bpd. That is nearly 1.5 percent of global refining capacity, according to the company.
The complex comprises two refineries: the original facility, commissioned in 1999 with a capacity of 660,000bpd, and a second, export-oriented refinery commissioned in 2008, adding 580,000bpd, which operates in a special economic zone.
Jamnagar imports crude from international suppliers and exports refined products to global markets. The refinery can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products.
Reliance said last month that the complex has processed more than 216 crude grades, claiming to be “perhaps the only refinery to achieve this feat”.
The Jamnagar refinery’s capacity is also driving a sharp revival in imports of Venezuelan crude — taken over by the US earlier this year after abducting then-President Nicolas Maduro — as Washington seeks to reshape global oil trade.
Reliance is expected to account for roughly 350,000bpd to 370,000bpd of the October intake, according to estimates from analytics firm Kpler. “We will talk with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude,” Rubio told reporters in brief remarks on Tuesday.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, right, with US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, in Mumbai, October 20, 2026 [Kylie Cooper/Reuters] Why is the refinery significant for global energy supplies?
Reliance is a central player in keeping global oil markets stable, as one of the world’s biggest suppliers of refined petroleum products. In September, for instance, six of the seven large cargo ships that docked at European Union ports carrying oil products were bearing Reliance goods.
Reliance’s biggest export is diesel, which Trump has been particularly worried about, with prices reaching historic highs in the US ahead of midterm elections early next month.
Though the data on exports by category is not public, an analysis by the Reuters news agency from trade sources noted that Reliance Industries exported 21.66 million tonnes of refined petroleum products in the first half of 2025 from Jamnagar. Diesel accounted for the largest share at 9.81 million tonnes, followed by petrol at 6.14 million tonnes and jet fuel at 2.06 million tonnes.
Europe accounted for the biggest share of the company’s exports, making up 28 percent of Reliance’s refined products during the period. Buyers include BP, ExxonMobil, Glencore, Vitol and Trafigura.
The Jamnagar refinery also shipped about $143m worth of oil products to the US last month, according to data cited by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank in Finland.
CREA noted in its report that the EU’s ban on importing petroleum products made from Russian crude from January 2026 does not adequately prevent products from refineries in third countries from entering Europe when those refineries also process Russian crude. The Jamnagar refinery is a prime example of that loophole.
Rubio’s visit to the refinery also comes as Trump faces his worst approval ratings amid inflation and rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm election in November. Just about 31 percent of Americans are happy with Trump’s performance – the lowest-ever number in his two terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey.
The Trump administration has also reportedly been pushing Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian energy facilities, which have rattled the global fuel markets.
Why the refinery is important for the Russia-Ukraine war
Reliance is also a critical actor in US efforts to influence how much oil Russia sells.
Since the start of Russia’s full-fledged war on Ukraine in February 2022, India has emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. And Reliance is driving that surge in imports. While only 3 percent of its oil was sourced from Russia before 2022, that share rose to 50 percent by 2025.
So when Trump imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to punish New Delhi for the purchase of Russian oil, Reliance was directly affected. It cut back on Russian crude imports significantly in subsequent months, but it still made up a third of the oil processed by Jamnagar’s refinery during the July-September 2026 quarter.
That was under threat when the Trump administration appeared poised to impose a 100 percent tariff on Indian goods because of continued Russian oil imports, under a new law passed last month.
But Trump has since suspended those proposed tariffs, easing concerns for India and Reliance.
Rubio has said India has been diversifying its import mix away from Russian crude, even as it still buys millions of barrels of Russian oil every day. “You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” Rubio said on Sunday.
“But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.”
Yes, India’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, the chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries, is investing in the US, primarily through energy-related projects.
It is backing America First Refining’s planned oil refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas, also the first major US refinery in about 50 years, announced by Trump in March.
The refinery is expected to cost $3bn to $4bn and process about 60 million barrels of US crude annually. Reliance has signed a 20-year agreement to buy a large share of the facility’s output, with operations expected to start around 2029.
In November 2024, Reliance’s US subsidiary also acquired a 21 percent stake in helium explorer Wavetech Helium for $12m as part of its low-carbon energy strategy.
Last month, Trump announced that India’s Essar Group — an oil major with knee-deep ties to Russia — is planning an $18bn integrated steel investment in the US through its subsidiary, Mesabi Metallics.
Despite Reliance’s investments in the US and Rubio’s upcoming visit to the Jamnagar facility, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man who is also a key Trump ally, recently hit out at Ambani.
His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.
In ⁠a series of X posts recently, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to ⁠favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio. Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing ‌him as “Prime ‌Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.
In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Edge Higher Amid Tech Rebound As Q3 Earnings Season Forges Ahead: DJT, AMZN, CBRS, CRWV Stocks In Focus
The run-up comes ahead of a busy earnings week that is likely to set the tone for technology stocks and the broader market.
Meta Platforms, Tesla, Lam Research, Texas Instruments, Bloom Energy, Valero Energy, and Netflix are among the top companies set to announce their quarterly prints this week.
Meanwhile, climbing oil prices amid growing geopolitical uncertainties have put some downward pressure on markets.
U.S. stock futures climbed into positive territory late Monday as technology stocks rebounded after a sharp selloff last week.
Meanwhile, markets are keenly watching the third-quarter (Q3) earnings season unfold, with about 70 S&P 500 companies slated to report earnings this week.

As of 11:13 p.m. EDT, Dow futures were up about 0.25%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.21% and the Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.15%.
On Monday, the three benchmark indexes closed mixed . The Nasdaq Composite led the climb, adding more than 290 points to close 1.11% higher. The S&P 500 climbed 0.41% at close, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.07%.
Technology and AI stocks were top of mind for markets on Monday as the sector reversed last week's steep selloff.
Chip stocks led the climb on Monday. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) closed up nearly 2%, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) closed up 1.61%. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Micron Technology Inc. (MU) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) all ended the session in green.
The run comes ahead of vital Q3 results that will follow this week, which are likely to set the tone for the trajectory of technology shares.
"Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration," Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays, said in a note, according to CNBC.
Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, reportedly said in a note on Monday that the week will be crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support, while noting that a hold is possible amid widespread, short-term oversold conditions.
Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) are due to report Q3 results later this week, while multiple other semiconductor and technology companies, including Lam Research (LRCX) and Texas Instruments (TXN), will also post their results.
AI-related power companies Bloom Energy (BE) and Valero Energy (VLO), along with big entertainment companies including Netflix Inc. (NFLX), will also announce their quarterly results.
Meanwhile, rising oil prices amid growing geopolitical uncertainty have put downward pressure on markets. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $109.88 a barrel, up about 0.3%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $103.64 per barrel.
Economist Peter Schiff said in a post on X, "Oil rose another 2.5% today. It's almost $104. If you think gas prices are high now, just wait until after the midterms when Trump has to turn off the spigots from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to keep it from running dry. Oil could hit $150, sending gas prices to record highs."
Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (DJT): Shares of the president's media company were in focus late Monday after the stock slipped 8%, its worst single-day drop since February, as President Donald Trump's approval rating hit a record low.
Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN): The company's stock surged nearly 5% at close on Monday and continued to climb higher overnight after Morgan Stanley raised its price target and named it a 'Top Pick.'
Cerebras Systems Inc. (CBRS): The AI hardware and supercomputing company was on the retail radar after shares slipped more than 5% on Monday, extending a broader selloff in the sector from last week.
CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV): Shares of the neocloud company fell more than 1% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names.
Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) all climbed overnight.
Meanwhile, U.S. long-dated Treasury yields continued above 5%. At the time of writing, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was 5.138%, and the 30-year Treasury yield was 5.473%.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.09% amid 'bullish' sentiment.
Asian markets opened lower on Tuesday, with South Korea's KOSPI, Japan's Nikkei 225, China's SSE Composite and Australian stocks all trading lower at the time of writing.

items.title: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction
items.summary: Copper is up 15.8% in 2026 as investors point to AI, grid and national security demand, tight supply and tariff-driven U.S. stockpiles.
items.content:
Why copper prices could withstand an AI spending slowdown
Copper has rallied nearly 16% this year, with strong demand driven by artificial intelligence, power grids and defense spending.
Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin says relatively “inelastic” demand from technology and defense could help copper withstand an AI-driven tech pullback.
U.S. tariff uncertainty, low Chinese inventories and tight supply are reinforcing investors’ bullish outlook for copper.
Copper is becoming increasingly strategic to governments and industries as artificial intelligence, power-grid investment and defense spending increase demand for the industrial metal, investors say.
The metal — a key component in electronics, construction and transportation, and often seen as a barometer of economic activity — has outperformed gold this year, as the need to secure reliable supplies has intensified.
Ivanhoe Electric's Melvin says copper can withstand a tech stock wobble
Copper has rallied 15.8% year-to-date, and is up more than 30% over the past 12 months. By comparison, gold futures have slipped 4.11% year-to-date, and are down 4.52% over the past 12 months. Spot gold is 4.89% lower over the past 12 months, and 4% down year-to-date.
Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin said countries, regions and industries are increasingly focused on securing access to metals for national security, economic growth and technology infrastructure. Melvin said that shift has helped support copper prices.
"It's certainly a good time to be in copper mining globally, and specifically in the United States," said Melvin, whose Arizona-based mining and exploration company focuses on copper, gold, silver, nickel and cobalt.
"We're really in a world right now where the metals that we used to refer to, and still do, as critical metals are really becoming strategic metals, in every sense of the word," said Melvin, who spoke as LME Week, the annual gathering of the global metals industry, began in London on Monday.
That shift comes as investors question the sustainability of AI spending and the hyperscaler build-out, which has led to a recent wobble in tech stocks.
But Melvin said he expects copper to withstand the recent volatility.
"It's a new pocket of demand, and it really is almost an inelastic demand for copper," he said of the tech sector's need for the metal. "It's hard to think that one of these large-scale technology companies is going to make an investment decision on a hyperscale data center based on the cost of copper."
He added: "That same inelasticity applies to another demand pocket that's emerging, which is national security, national defense budgets. So when you look at copper demand, the impact of technology, artificial intelligence infrastructure, I think we can all agree that that market is growing.
"There certainly has been a bit of a retrench, a retreat, in those [tech] valuations. But two things can be true at the same time — you can have a capital market move in sentiment on equity values… but it can also be true that those industries are growing, and they're going to be a source of incremental demand for our metal."
The rally has also been supported by uncertainty over whether the U.S. will impose a tariff on refined copper. In 2025, the Commerce Department recommended a 15% tariff beginning Jan. 1, 2027, but no final decision on the proposed levy has been publicly announced.
"Because of the potential for US tariffs, a large share of the world's copper is now stored in the U.S., and it isn't clear those stocks will be available to the rest of the market," said Iain Pyle, senior investment director at Aberdeen Investments and co-manager of the abrdn Future Minerals Fund.
"At the same time, Chinese inventories look exceptionally low and premiums there are rising."
In an Oct. 15 note, Pyle called copper the "clearest example" of a market where supply cannot keep up with demand. "Higher incentives will be needed in the form of sustained higher copper prices.
"There is still some risk of a pullback around tariff announcements, but we see the underlying fundamentals as clearly bullish, and the potential for a spike in prices has increased."

Nvidia vs. TSMC: Which Business Depends Less on Picking the Winning AI Chip?
Nvidia and TSMC both appear in our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade , but they offer different answers to a long-term problem: what happens if the winning AI-chip architecture changes? Owning a manufacturer can spread that technology bet, although it introduces a different set of concentrated risks. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) sells a computing platform built around its chips, networking and software. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM ) manufactures customers' designs. They are alternative ways to own AI-computing growth, not direct substitutes in the supply chain.
Nvidia vs. TSMC: Which Business Depends Less on Picking the Winning AI Chip? Courtesy of NVIDIA
TSMC's advantage is conditional neutrality: it can earn manufacturing revenue from competing customers when their designs use its processes. A shift toward custom accelerators could therefore leave manufacturing demand intact even if it pressures a merchant-chip supplier. The inference depends on where the replacement chips are made; it is not proof that TSMC captures every design win.
Its third-quarter results reported 79% of wafer revenue from technologies at seven nanometers and below. Two-nanometer products contributed 8%, demonstrating an ongoing process transition. Maintaining that position requires yields, reliable delivery and expensive capacity. Our TSMC-ASML expansion comparison explains how much cash ownership of the factories can consume.
Nvidia's opposing strength is that customers buy usable computing, not merely transistor capacity. Its ecosystem and system integration can preserve demand even when another chip looks attractive on an isolated specification. The risk is that customers develop enough software and custom hardware to reduce what they pay for that integration.
Diversification changes the risk rather than removing it
Nvidia's latest quarter generated $89 billion of data-center revenue out of $96.22 billion total, about 92.5%. That concentration creates powerful exposure to infrastructure spending. A broad customer roster would not eliminate a shared customer-capital-spending shock.
TSMC reported a 58.7% operating margin in its latest quarter, but a foundry's customer diversity does not diversify away factory location or utilization. If demand falls across designers, the manufacturer still owns the capacity. Our geographic-risk comparison examines why changing the point of entry into the chip supply chain does not automatically remove Taiwan exposure.
Using October 16 prices, Nvidia's equity value was about 41 times trailing cash after capital expenditure. The equity value implied by TSMC's U.S. depositary-share price was about 47 times, using five ordinary shares per depositary share. These historical cash multiples include different investment cycles; they are not evidence that the foundry is automatically the cheaper route.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders increased to 285 from 275 for Nvidia and to 249 from 234 for TSMC. Fisher added 3% to Nvidia shares, and Fisher increased TSMC shares 2%. Nvidia's September 30 short interest was 1.35% of float.
TSMC offers less dependence on a single merchant-computing architecture, provided it retains the manufacturing work. Nvidia offers greater exposure to the value of an integrated platform. The choice turns on whether an investor is more confident in platform economics or manufacturing leadership, while separately accounting for valuation and geography.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of NVDA and TSM as investments, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Jim Cramer's top 10 things to watch in the stock market Tuesday
My top 10 things to watch Tuesday, Oct. 20 1. Nasdaq futures are under pressure this morning after yesterday's bounce-back rally. Spillover from South Korea's Kospi again? Seoul-based neocloud Elice plunged 32% in its market debut, pressuring the broader artificial intelligence trade. Seems extreme on the downside, but the deal was placed really badly in a bad tape. 2. Oil is not helping things today. WTI crude for December delivery is up over 2% to nearly $101 a barrel, and international benchmark Brent is up almost 2% to trade north of $111, its highest price since May. With oil rampaging and the data-center cohort (including CoreWeave ) weak thanks to some little-known South Korean company, is this just a Johnson & Johnson kind of day? 3. GE Aerospace reported some very strong numbers, but shares are off 3%. Top and bottom line beats, with orders up 49%, which is practically unheard of. Not just commercial either. Defense orders look strong too. The engine maker also upped its full-year guide for adjusted profit, revenue growth, operating income and free cash flow. RTX Corp's earnings were also better than expected this morning. Good read-throughs for Club name Boeing . 4. General Motors is down more than 7% despite reporting better-than-expected revenue and adjusted earnings, and announcing a $20 billion stock buyback program. Boosted its free cash flow outlook, but it's seeing inflationary pressures, including logistics and memory chips. The company said in its earnings slides "the path forward is more challenging," but expects a strong 2027 assuming resilient demand and moderating cost pressures. 5. 3M is up about 1% after third-quarter revenue matched essentially expectations, but earnings topped consensus. Adjusted EPS was up 12% year over year, the third quarter in a row of double-digit growth. Buybacks are helping here. Innovation is working, with five-year new product sales up 34% year to date. CEO Bill Brown is seeing results two-plus years into his tenure. 6. Morgan Stanley raised its Seagate price target to $1,200 from $1,187 and kept its buy rating. The analysts reinstated the storage stock as their "top pick" in IT hardware. However, they lowered their Western Digital price target to $643 from $676, while keeping their buy rating. They see no cessation of demand. They expect beat-and-raise quarters from both. 7. Loop Capital downgraded its rating on Club name Apple to hold from buy and cut its price target to $330 from $370. On its last earnings call, Apple noted that supply constraints will impact iPhones. Now, Loop is worried the demand won't be there next year to compensate. After its recent surge to record highs, the analysts argued that Apple stock needs a "fundamental catalyst reset. "Is this note trying to get ahead of cuts? 8. Another day, another price target boost for Club name Eli Lilly . Following Bank of America's move yesterday, Goldman Sachs went to $1,413 from $1,371 and kept its buy rating. Goldman expects Lilly to deliver a beat-and-raise print next week, helped by international GLP-1 sales ( a key source of upside lately). Just how big will the guidance raise be? That's the debate. 9. Williams-Sonoma picked up a pair of price target hikes. Piper Sandler went to $286 from $259 and reiterated its buy recommendation. Evercore ISI went to $255 from $240, though it stayed at a hold. Been a tough year for most consumer discretionary stocks, but not for Williams-Sonoma . Shares are up almost 40% in 2026. CEO Laura Alber has done a remarkable job despite a terrible housing market. 10. ServiceNow was named a top pick at BMO Capital Markets, and Bernstein raised its price target to $266 from $248. That implies some serious upside (83% to be exact) from yesterday's close of $145.36. The comeback for enterprise software names has been incredible. Almost as if the "SaaSpocalypse" narrative was nonsense. ServiceNow reports earnings next Wednesday evening. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy hugs US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff next to Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish president Alexander Stubb in Oslo, Norway. Photograph: Heiko Junge/Reuters The intensity of the attacks on western Ukraine is such that neighbouring Poland has issued as many as four security alerts today to residents in the south-east of the country, with the latest warning of immediate danger and instructing people to shelter in place. It was cancelled some 20 minutes later.
A spokesperson for the Polish army confirmed that a drone was detected 15 kilometres from the Polish border, prompting the alarm, but Polish airspace did not get violated, Onet reported.

Romania's prime minister Luca Niculescu delivers a speech before a confidence vote on his cabinet during a plenary session of the Parliament assembly in Bucharest, Romania. Photograph: Robert Ghement/EPA Niculescu, a former journalist and diplomat who served as Romania’s ambassador to France , is expected to form a government led by ministers from the centre-left Social Democratic party and some technocrats – although it remains a very open question how long he will last in the post.
Back to France , the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told lawmakers of plans for “massive” deployment of police forces ahead of further protests expected on Saturday.
France's prime minister Sébastien Lecornu looks on during a session of questions to the government at the French National Assembly, French Parliament's lower house, in Paris. Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty Images In a passionate speech in the parliament, Lecornu framed the situation as a choice “between violence the Republic,” as he doubled down on his claims that the protests morphed into “an insurrectionary scheme led by far-left and ultra-left groups.”
He insisted that “a return to order is the prerequisite for everything else,” stressing he also wants to address the substantive requests posed by the student movement.
He also acknowledged some issues with the police planning and intelligence gathering so far.
Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto has warned that recent riots in Milan and other parts of Italy were part of a broader “hybrid war” against the West, the Italian news agency Ansa reported.
Defence minister Guido Crosetto in the Senate during Question time in Rome. Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/Shutterstock Speaking at a conference in Rome, Crosetto said:
“ The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras; they are the product of what I call hybrid warfare – a form of conflict being waged against our nations through unconventional tools like TikTok, social media, and YouTube … The West has yet to realise this or take any meaningful action in response.”
“If three out of every 10 young people took part in these demonstrations – and I am not just referring to ‘maranza’ (youth gangs) or second-generation Italians – and if six out of 10 agree with these sentiments, it is because they have been subjected to a ‘counter-education’ from somewhere – not from their families or schools.
This has instilled in them values, ambitions, a worldview, and points of reference that stand in direct conflict with the society we live in and with our democratic rules.”
As we mentioned in a previous post , US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy which are aimed at ending the war with Russia.
It comes as relations between Zelenskyy and the US president, Donald Trump, are at their lowest since their public fallout in the Oval Office last year .
Only yesterday, Zelenskyy said the US was deliberately delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, deepening the public spat with Trump. He has also said that Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening.
As the diplomacy in Oslo takes place to end the war, we are seeing more reports of deadly Russian attacks on Ukraine. Four people were killed and 27 others injured, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, according to regional police.
Three people were killed and six were injured in the Obukhiv district , where warehouses were damaged, police said. This morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway , Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.
Meanwhile, Portuguese police cleared protest camps in ⁠Lisbon and Porto before ⁠dawn, removing activists who had occupied two central squares to protest against a worsening housing crisis, and making 55 arrests, Reuters reported.
Activists ⁠had occupied Lisbon’s Rossio square since Saturday, pitching around 200 tents, and Porto’s Dom Joao I square for around 10 days.
Dozens of tents are pictured during a encampment set up in protest against housing shortage, soaring rents and low wages, at Rossio square in central Lisbon. Photograph: Patrícia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty Images The ⁠camps mirrored housing protests in neighbouring Spain, and coincided with unrest over rising ​living costs in countries such as ‌ France , Belgium and Italy.
Italy is poised to approve new security measures after parts of the country were rocked by waves of protests over the weekend.
Italy’s deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini , said that as part of the crackdown police will be able to detain under-18s at police stations for 12 hours, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger.
“We want to intervene quickly on young people,” Salvini told the RTL ​radio broadcaster ahead of a cabinet meeting to approve the measures, which have not yet been formally announced.
The security crackdown will also reportedly include banning gatherings for people deemed a threat to public order.
Thousands of people peacefully protested against living costs in cities across northern Italy over the weekend, but a number of the marches turned violent with some demonstrators seen looting stores and clashing with police.
Several hundred protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze ‌and looted shops in the centres of Milan, where more than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend.
In southern Italy, farmers and truckers have been blockading ports and highways to protest against the surge in fuel prices resulting from the US-Israel war on Iran.
Police officers in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy, on 18 October 2026. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock France will offer interest-free loans of up to €50,000 to businesses affected by the riots and looting over the weekend, economy minister Roland Lescure said.
The scheme is expected to open on Friday, and should help traders with cash flow issues as they seek to get insurance payouts, the minister said, quoted by French media.
A supermarket in Paris’s 10th arrondissement, which was left in a state of disarray following this weekend’s riots. Photograph: Paoloni Jeremy/ABACA/Shutterstock First court cases are also being progressed, with justice minister Gérald Darmanin confirming that 149 people have been put in provisional detention or imprisoned as part of ongoing trials. In a separate TV appearance on Monday evening, he said around 2,500 remained in custody for questioning, Reuters reported.
The number is expected to go up, as BFMTV reported that some 40 people are expected to appear in front of Parisian courts this afternoon.
French Police officers arrest a protester during a demonstration against the rising cost of living and cuts to public services in Paris. Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPA In other news, it looks like France may have another problem coming its way, with heavy rainfall in the south of the country.
Parts of Corsica are now under a red alert for rain and flooding, with local flooding observed last night in several towns and village in the region. An all-time rainfall record broken in Salon-de-Provence, BFMTV reported.
The Gard department is on orange alert, with the coastal areas on a yellow alert.

People line up to refill gas bottles at a refilling station in Taiz on Monday. Fighting is under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the city. Photograph: Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP/Getty Images
Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Map of Yemen Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
A person walks past bodies on the ground Bodies lie on the ground after the explosion at al-Alam camp in Yemen The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting bug had Saudi support, claims prosecutors
items.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, who is accused of planting a recording device, has been denied bail.
items.content:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing , external in California.
US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the ChatGPT-maker, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and said a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
The 35-year-old engineer was deemed a flight risk and denied bail on Monday, pending a trial.
The Saudi government did not respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.
The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.
Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.
On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".
Alfozan was scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.
The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.
A container from the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride floats alongside small motorboats after the ship sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: Social media/Reuters Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates , sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”
Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.
The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman , a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ( IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.
Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.
It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.
A satellite image shows containers and items floating in the water after the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/Reuters Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.
Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief. Photograph: Reuters On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.
“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.
Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.
Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.
Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

items.title: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?
items.summary: Analysts say a Russian craft’s close pass by a commercial radar satellite is a first and a warning to Kyiv’s backers.
items.content:
Share Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? on social media
An artilleryman of the Special Rifle Police Battalion of Zaporizhzhia region sets up Starlink satellite internet system, at a position in Ukraine [File: Reuters]
A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, a US defence news site.
Cosmos 2612 may have passed ICEYE-X36, a satellite owned by the US arm of the Finnish company ICEYE.
