LeoLabs, a US space-tracking company, put the closest approach at about 500 metres, according to Breaking Defence.
ICEYE has supplied radar imagery to Ukraine since 2022, Defence News reported.
So is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? Al Jazeera spoke to analysts to find out:
A Russian satellite has deliberately positioned itself close to a Western one, after months of manoeuvring.
Cosmos 2612 is one of six satellites the Russian military launched in April, The War Zone reported.
In May, four of them moved close to an ICEYE satellite.
ICEYE-X36 is a commercial satellite, owned by a private company rather than a government, but ICEYE sells radar imagery to militaries and supplies data to the US and its allies.
ICEYE’s chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told the Reuters news agency the company then moved its own satellite, which appeared to prompt further Russian manoeuvres.
Then, between Thursday and Friday last week, Cosmos 2612 closed in from more than 320km (200 miles) from ICEYE-X36 to about 4.8km (3 miles), the space-tracking company LeoLabs told the news site Axios.
Over the weekend, it moved between positions ahead of and behind the ICEYE satellite, at times coming within roughly 500 metres, LeoLabs said in a report on Monday, adding that the estimate was uncertain and, by Monday, it had begun to move away.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Ukraine’s military works with ICEYE and uses its capabilities, but said it was unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine.
Has Russia done this before, and what is the purpose?
In the past, Russia has mainly carried out such manoeuvres against Western military satellites, rather than commercially owned ones, Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in the defence studies department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
In early 2020, two Russian satellites moved close to USA 245, a US spy satellite.
In September 2025, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said two Russian Luch-Olymp satellites were tracking two Intelsat satellites used by the German military.
Dr Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in optical space situational awareness at TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, said: “At geostationary altitude, we have seen two Russian satellites (LUCH/OLYMP-K 1 & 2) repeatedly approach western communication satellites to distances of a few tens of kilometres in the past few years, likely with the intention to eavesdrop on communications and data transfers. And we have seen the Russians practising very close approaches in Low Earth Orbit – similar to what they now did to ICEYE-X36 – with their own satellites as test targets.”
However, this incident is different, because “approaching another satellite this close without the cooperation of the owner or operator of the other satellite, is widely considered ‘not done’ as it is dangerous, with a risk of collision or interference.
“It is equivalent to placing your car on the freeway within 10 cm of another driving car: highly unsafe.”
Langbroek said it is not known what the purpose of the Russian manoeuvre was, however, “it could be a dry run for a future attack, it could be provocation or scare tactics to ruffle the feathers of Ukraine and its allies, and/or a test to see how the satellite operators react to a threat like this.”
This sort of manoeuvre, therefore, falls into the pattern of “hybrid warfare” – “the same kind of provocations and inciting reactions like what Russia does when they fly a drone into Polish airspace or zoom a NATO warship at low elevation in the Baltic Sea”.
Close approaches have happened for years, but not like this.
Hilborne said this is “the first time that a country has done such a manoeuvre … against the commercial satellite without any consent”.
It was also “incredibly close”, he said, with some reports putting the distance at less than 30 metres.
Far more common is interference that does not require going near a satellite at all. This is mostly done through jamming, which drowns out a satellite’s signals, often from the ground.
Western military officials told Reuters that Russian interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
For Hilborne, the choice of target “is starting to indicate that Russia does not distinguish between commercial and military satellites as potential targets”.
That matters because militaries, including Ukraine’s, increasingly rely on commercial satellites for communications and imagery.
In October 2022, a senior Russian foreign ministry official told the United Nations that “quasi-civilian infrastructure may be a legitimate target for a retaliatory strike”.
Juliana Suess, a space security researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, said Russia may be calculating that reactions will be less severe if it shadows a commercial satellite rather than a sovereign one, especially one not belonging to the US.
ICEYE-X36 is owned by ICEYE’s US subsidiary and registered as a US satellite, Hilborne noted, adding, “this creates a complex problem”.
The distance matters too. A gap of less than 5km may sound far, Suess said, but “it’s essentially a hop and a skip in space”.
“It’s incredibly close and could potentially enable Russia to conduct nefarious activity, including intercepting data from the satellite or disrupting its service – temporarily via signal jamming, for example,” she added.
“A kinetic attack would also be possible but seems less likely at this point in time, in part because this would be an unprecedented measure taken against a satellite”, she explained.
“It is sending a message that these platforms could be held under threat,” Hilborne said, adding that it also represents an escalation, suggesting Russia might be willing to attack, since any satellite could be used as a weapon simply by crashing it into another.
Suess added: “I think regardless of whether we see further manoeuvring or consequences, the political goal of intimidation should not be underestimated”.
“The manoeuvre is also a message that space assets cannot be considered wholly safe or removed from the war in Ukraine”, she said.
She pointed to November 2021, when Russia destroyed one of its own satellites with a missile, an event referred to in the European Union’s 2023 space strategy.
“We have long known what Russia is capable of in terms of disrupting or even destroying space assets. This manoeuvre is also a reminder of those previously demonstrated capabilities,” she said.
Moscow calls such spacecraft “inspector satellites”, and in 2020 described such manoeuvres as common practice “by many countries”, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported.
Hilborne described the approach as “another example of activity that sits below the threshold of conflict”.
An outright attack on ICEYE-X36 looks unlikely for now, Hilborne said.
“With the current balance in the conflict, and this being an American-registered satellite, it would seem unlikely that Russia would actually attack the satellite, as the response would be unpredictable”, he said.
An attack could also create a large amount of space debris, which would be a problem for everyone, he added, warning that “it’s hard to second-guess where Russia draws the line”.
Ukraine’s access to satellites has come under pressure before, at times from its own allies.
In March 2025, as Washington paused intelligence sharing with Kyiv, the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency “temporarily suspended” Ukraine’s access to the main portal for US government-purchased commercial imagery.
If ICEYE-X36 were disrupted, Ukraine would not necessarily go blind, Suess said, because the ICEYE constellation has more than one satellite, and sovereign radar satellites, such as Germany’s, could also provide data.
But speed is the issue. According to ICEYE, the expanded access agreed this year meant faster access, Suess explained.
“The question is whether a similarly fast transfer of data could be enabled with a new provider, whether commercial or sovereign in nature,” she said.
Now, Ukraine faces another squeeze. Last week, the order to limit Starshield – the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service – for Ukraine came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official told Reuters.
On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Starshield is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but that Kyiv’s request to use it for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.

items.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
items.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
items.content:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media reports.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on the "S" list, a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFMTV reported.
Meanwhile in Marseille, a curfew for young people will be introduced on Tuesday evening.
The city's mayor BenoÃ®t Payan said that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew in Marseille "starting this evening and for days to come".
He said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.
French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".
But French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.
Image caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire
Targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.
Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
Image caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night
Earlier Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.
Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.
Image caption, Riots took place across French cities, including the capital Paris
More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.
Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.
The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
Meanwhile, French union La CGT has called for a major day of strikes on 5 November.

Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
Trump defends decision to waive some sanctions on Russia; Lithuania foils attack on Starlink site; Kyiv hits another oil terminal. What we know on day 1,699
Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries , but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones.
Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”. He added: “It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.”
In September, a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablaze with Warsaw claiming sabotage. In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way amid claims that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire .
Shipping Russian diesel to the US market will take 15 to 20 days once contracts are signed , a senior Russian official said on Sunday, though a date for signing has yet to be announced. Trump announced the controversial agreement with Moscow last week, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections. “Negotiations are currently under way regarding the commercial terms – that is, on finalisation of the contracts,” Russian deputy prime minister for energy Alexander Novak said in an interview with state media. “Once the contracts are signed, the fuel will reach the markets – in this case, the US markets – within 15 to 20 days.”
Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. One person was killed and five others were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, officials said. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre operated by Russian tech company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed. Russia’s defence ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

items.title: Warren Buffett Is Issuing a Stark Warning About the Stock Market. Here's What History Says Comes Next. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Warren Buffett Is Issuing a Stark Warning About the Stock Market. Here's What History Says Comes Next.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
This year has been one for the record books, with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.29% ) , Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +0.07% ) , and Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.76% ) all reaching multiple all-time highs.
But what goes up must come down eventually. Bond yields are at their highest levels in decades, raising borrowing costs for consumers and making debt more expensive for companies spending billions of dollars on the AI build-out . Concerns about AI debt have shaken the market recently, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq experiencing its worst week in months.
While nobody can say for certain what will happen in the near term, Warren Buffett issued a warning earlier this year about this historically expensive market -- and history suggests he's right.
In a CNBC interview earlier this year, Buffett was asked how investors should navigate these historically high stock prices. He warned that some investors are getting too comfortable with unsafe investments and risk overpaying for stocks.
"I've compared the markets to a church with a casino attached, [and] the casino has gotten very attractive to people," he warned. "So we've never had people in a more gambling mood than now."
He went on to add, however, that "that doesn't mean that investing is terrible. It does mean that prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly."
Many stocks are currently at record high prices. While that's not inherently a bad thing, some stocks are being fueled primarily by hype and speculation rather than fundamentals . These stocks can sometimes perform well in the short term, but they carry far more risk than companies built on solid foundations.
The stock market will always be unpredictable to a degree, but one market indicator with a strong track record of calling previous downturns is the S&P 500 Shiller Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE) Ratio.
This metric tracks the S&P 500's long-term valuation using the index's 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings. The higher the ratio climbs, the more likely that the market is overvalued. The CAPE Ratio also has an inverse relationship with stock prices, as higher metrics tend to be followed by lower prices.
The last time this ratio surged was in late 2021, when it peaked at 38 just before stocks fell into a bear market that would last most of the following year. But it also spiked sharply in 1929 (ahead of the Great Depression) and 1999 (during the dot-com bubble).
Currently, the ratio is above 40 and has held above that benchmark since May of this year. That's historically significant, because the only other time this metric has stayed above 40 for months at a time was during the dot-com bubble. It surpassed 40 in January 1999, peaked at around 44 in December, and the bear market officially began in March 2000.
To be clear, 40 isn't some magical threshold that automatically triggers bear markets. Also, no market metric can predict when a downturn will begin. But it's unusual for the market to be this richly valued, and it suggests that many stocks are trading at a premium right now.
The single best move investors can make right now is to ensure they're buying quality stocks with solid fundamentals. Then, prepare to hold those stocks for at least a few years.
Some stocks are overvalued right now , and those investments have the most to lose during a bear market. When the dot-com bubble popped, for instance, many high-flying tech stocks that were breaking records in the 1990s crashed hard and never recovered.
As Buffett said, though, not all investing is terrible. The best investments aren't always the flashy stocks making headlines. Sometimes they're the hidden gems in overlooked industries. While even the healthiest stocks can take a hit during a market downturn, they're more likely to recover over time.

items.title: What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests
items.summary: Protests broke out in France and several European countries as people railed against living costs, poor schooling conditions, and a housing crisis.
items.content:
Why violent protests are sweeping across Europe over living costs
Violent protests have erupted in several European countries over dissatisfaction with living costs.
Demonstrations in France saw protesters set city halls ablaze and attack police officers.
"The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S.," a Portuguese minister told CNBC.
Protesters march through central Paris amid fires, smoke, police deployments and clashes during nationwide demonstrations against the high cost of living, on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France.
Anger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has brought hundreds of thousands of protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities.
France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, with more than 500,000 people marching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers.
Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent.
There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC. The increase in energy costs may be playing a role, but the increase is smaller than in 2022, at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, when there were no comparable violent protests, he added.
Nevertheless, the demonstrations pose a shared challenge for governments: how to improve living conditions and maintain public services while supporting households and keeping strained public finances in check.
The demonstrations in France began last month when high school students criticized poor schooling conditions, including shoddy facilities and teacher shortages. They have since evolved into broader protests over living standards and declining public services.
In Spain, housing protests began in September after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted following a 230% rent increase by an investment fund. She died a fortnight later.
Thousands of protesters also took to the streets in Portugal on Saturday to demonstrate against soaring housing costs and the cost of living.
"People obviously are protesting on the cost of living with diesel and fuel prices, but mainly on housing costs, which have been increasing substantially all over Europe, but also particularly in Portugal," Miranda Sarmento, Portugal's minister of state and finance, said Monday.
Portugal Fin Min: France shouldn't suffer same fiscal pain that we did
In Albania, protesters were angry about poor university conditions and high tuition fees, and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Some threw Molotov cocktails and other objects at the police and set fire to cars and litter bins.
In Italy, a march in central Milan on Saturday over living costs also ended violently, with rioters attacking the police with stones and paving blocks and setting fire to barricades.
"The underlying problem is that politicians are not able to offer hope of a better life for many Europeans because the economy is growing only slowly and governments have built up huge debts, leaving them little scope to support higher public spending or to cut taxes," Capital Economics' Kenningham said.
The escalation of violence in France in particular is due to a "conjugation of different elements," said Douglas Yates, a professor at the American Graduate School in Paris.
"This was a storm that turned into a hurricane," Yates told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick. "There was this inflation, which has brought out the cost-of-living protesters who would have been disgruntled at any rate."
Yates said another factor is France's 2027 presidential election, as opposition parties seek to capitalize on growing public discontent with President Emmanuel Macron .
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a 2027 budget aimed at narrowing France's deficit , projected at 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. Measures include freezing the civil service pay index and tightening reimbursement for sick leave.
"Finally there's the students, the poor students who started this by making reasonable demands for having their dilapidated infrastructure repaired and perhaps getting some air conditioners installed in the classrooms, and so these three forces have come together and created an out-of-control hurricane," Yates added.
The economic backdrop has also deteriorated. In the second quarter of 2026, France's unemployment rate rose to 8.3%, representing 2.7 million people, according to Insee, the national statistics bureau . The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds climbed to 21.6%.
Consumer prices rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August, according to final Insee data. Energy prices jumped 21.3%. Meanwhile, purchasing power per consumption unit is projected to fall 0.7% in 2026, according to Insee figures, cited by Le Monde .
Calculations by the French Institute of Economics for Le Monde estimate that the decline in purchasing power since 2024 is equivalent to a loss of 1,200 euros ($1,345) a year for a household with two adults and two children, and 600 euros for a single adult.
During the demonstration on 17 October in Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges Haute-Vienne in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France on 17 October 2026.
Portugal's Sarmento said that the situation across Europe varies, with Portugal in a stronger fiscal position and with much less debt than France.
"Those countries [those with higher public debt] have much less fiscal margin to act, but the main issue is that we need to resolve the problem of productivity and competitiveness at the European level," he said.
"The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S., and without economic growth, it's impossible to have better salaries and to have the resources for better public services and social support," Sarmento added.
In the second quarter of 2026, Portugal recorded the EU's highest annual increase in house prices, up 16.5% from a year earlier, according to Eurostat .
The Portuguese government is looking to increase the supply of housing to reduce buying and renting costs to resolve the issue, according to Sarmento.
French government bond yields rose and the euro weakened on Monday as the unrest added to investor concerns over France's debt and budget.
"It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
"Taxes could well go up for French businesses. I think taxes may generally go up in France. Fiscal consolidation means you need to either spend less or tax more. Those things are very tricky."
Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said France faced a "very real risk" of a sovereign debt crisis.
"What's needed in France is to get the fiscal position in order; they need to raise the retirement age — you can't retire at 62 if the average person's living to 84 — but if this is going on even before they start talking about that, then imagine what would happen on the streets of France if you tried to raise the retirement age... I mean, here in the U.K. it's 68," Bell added.

items.title: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war - CBS News
items.summary: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war  CBS News
items.content:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed in an X post that he was in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility on Monday, sharing a photo of himself addressing American service members who he said were "on a historic mission." He did not specify his location or mention Israel.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.
Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.
Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections .
Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu told Israeli media last week he is not planning to launch renewed strikes against Iran before the Oct. 27 elections, saying , "it is not convenient for us."
Mr. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday , calling him "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
The U.S. president has maintained a close relationship with Netanyahu, though he has put pressure on Israel at times. Over the spring and summer, the Trump administration urged Israel to ease up on striking Lebanon, home to Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
The administration has also encouraged Israel to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank and cut a longer-term deal with Hamas in the Gaza Strip.
Last month, Trump envoy Jared Kushner suggested the upcoming Israeli elections may have delayed progress in Gaza, saying at a conference in Kyiv: "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."

items.title: Residents warned not to drink tap water after hundreds fall sick near South Africa capital
items.summary: More than 400 people, mostly children, become ill after drinking contaminated water, east of Pretoria.
items.content:
Image caption, Tests found traces of E. coli in water supplied to residents living near Pretoria
Residents living near South Africa's capital, Pretoria, have been warned not to drink or cook with tap water after more than 400 people, mostly children under four, fell ill after drinking contaminated water.
The cases were detected in Tshwane, the area which includes Pretoria, after people reported to their local hospital with "stomach cramps and diarrhoea" over a two-week period, officials said.
No deaths have been reported but high levels of E. coli were found in the water.
Tshwane has faced numerous outbreaks from waterborne diseases in recent years. In 2023, 29 people were killed by a cholera outbreak in a township just outside Pretoria.
That outbreak, in Hammanskraal, was linked to substandard water purification practices.
In 2025, officials confirmed 48 cases of typhoid in the same area east of Pretoria. The source of the outbreak remains unclear.
No cholera bacteria has been found in the latest cases.
The departments of water and health, in a joint statement on Monday, said 408 cases had been detected between 7 and 18 October in about five townships.
They said that lab tests "indicate that the illness has been caused by residents being exposed to contaminated water" from a local water treatment facility supplying water to several communities east of Pretoria.
Samples tested found norovirus, campylobacter, shigella and "other pathogens that cause stomach cramps and diarrhoea", officials said.
The team's early investigations found that local authorities had failed to warn residents about the contaminated water.
The water supplied to the area has been declared unfit for human consumption and authorities urged residents to only use it to flush toilets. Tankers have been dispatched to supply clean drinking water.
"Previously stored water should be discarded, and water containers must be disinfected using household bleach," officials said.

Data center stocks slide as Korea IPO plunges 30%, pressuring tech sentiment
Shares of cloud provider Elice Group dropped 30% during their market debut in South Korea.
Elice Group has been compared to CoreWeave, the U.S. neocloud at the center of last week's sell-off.
Concerns about overcapacity in computing power amid lackluster AI revenues are persisting.
Data center stocks struggled Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave.
Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity.
The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities. CoreWeave shares lost 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 4%. Iren was down about 6%.
HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away.
"Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds ," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside.
Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters . Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses.
Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out.
Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates.
Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note.
Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030.
"Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said.
Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC.
"At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."
Chip stocks are also feeling some pain on Tuesday. Micron is down close to 2% as of market open; AMD is down about 1.5%; and Nvidia is down about 1%.

items.title: AI chip stocks bounce back as hyperscaler earnings loom, META equity raise in focus - 24/7 Wall St.
items.summary: AI chip stocks bounce back as hyperscaler earnings loom, META equity raise in focus  24/7 Wall St.
items.content:
AI chip stocks bounce back as hyperscaler earnings loom, META equity raise in focus
NVIDIA collects a check whether hyperscalers borrow, issue stock, or drain their cash reserves, but Meta faces a funding squeeze that could reshape what shareholders actually own. The size of one expected equity offering may decide how this AI spending…
This graphic illustrates the interconnectedness of advanced optical technology, like that developed by Lumentum, with significant market and investment growth. © Shutterstock
Chip stocks bounced on October 19, and the session showed who collects the money in this AI cycle. The Nasdaq rose 1.3% with semiconductors leading; NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) gained 1.38%, and Meta Platforms ( NASDAQ:META ) slipped 0.55%.
Seema Mody's segment that day focused on that split. The GPU supplier rose while the hyperscaler expected to raise outside money fell behind, although one session cannot show that equity talk drove Meta lower.
Meta's expansion now needs more than its own cash. It guided 2026 capital expenditures to $130 billion to $145 billion, and second-quarter free cash flow fell to $784 million from $8.55 billion a year earlier.
NVIDIA reported $96.22 billion in quarterly revenue, up 105.8%. That gap between the buyer's falling cash and the seller's rising sales is why the coming hyperscaler reports carry more weight than a typical quarter.
Why This Pullback Could Precede Strong Hyperscaler Reports
Mody cited Evercore ISI: "Evercore ISI out with a note this morning that leans a bit more bullish saying the pullback that we've recently seen in these names comes ahead of what they think will be a strong hyperscaler earnings season." The firm reads recent weakness as a setup for those reports.
NVIDIA is still down 4.08% over the past week and 2.33% over the past month, although it is up 16.67% year to date.
Meta fell 5.05% over the past week and is down 1.28% over the past year despite a 7.13% gain in 2026. The weak one-year return suggests some investors likely doubt the payoff from the spending.
Watch capital spending plans, AI revenue, and how the spending gets financed. NVIDIA expects top five hyperscaler capex to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026.
Mody noted: "The H100 that's Nvidia's older chip has held up in terms of pricing ever since Anthropic's latest model came out." New model launches are lifting demand for older hardware too.
That signals demand for compute still exceeds supply. NVIDIA said it has supply for about 70% of demand.
It also protects collateral, because GPUs now back loans. Chips that hold their rental rates also hold their value as loan collateral.
Asia is more cautious: "Bank of America's semiconductor team just returning from Asia, sharing with clients that investors there are a bit more anxious about the AI funding cycle." The worry there centers on funding.
Mody said: "Consensus amongst credit folks we spoke to over the weekend is that GPU backed loans will be the go to option for these companies. Unsecured debt will be less desirable, especially at 15%." That shifts financing risk onto chip values.
Unsecured borrowing near 15% makes long-dated data centers hard to justify. Secured loans cost less because lenders can claim the hardware.
Nebius Group ( NASDAQ:NBIS ) entered its first senior secured facility, about $775 million backed by GPUs and contracted cash flows, in July 2026. If used GPU prices fall, the collateral declines and lenders tighten terms.
Analysts expect a Meta stock sale, and Mody said the open issue is size: "The biggest question is not whether META will issue stock, but how big META's equity offering could be. They say the market is comfortable for 30 billion." Meta has not announced an offering.
Alphabet  ( NASDAQ:GOOG , NASDAQ:GOOGL ) completed an $80 billion stock issuance a couple of months ago. Dilution spreads future profits across more owners.
Meta's apps reach over 3.6 billion daily active people. AI spending is exceeding even that level of cash generation.
Long-term debt already reached $83.66 billion, and issuing stock would likely let Meta avoid borrowing near 15%.
The size and terms of Meta's raise remain unknown, which leaves the valuation case uncertain. At $705.44 and a trailing P/E of 26, dilution and an open-ended spending cap limit upside for existing holders.
NVIDIA sits in a different position. At $217.09 and a trailing P/E of 44, it costs more, but it gets paid whether buyers use stock, GPU-backed loans, or cash.
Steady H100 pricing points to durable demand, and NVIDIA guided third-quarter revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%.
A smaller-than-expected raise or clear AI revenue disclosure from Meta would ease concerns about dilution and its spending payoff. Hyperscaler earnings will show whether either arrives.

Investing.com -- European chip stocks opened lower Tuesday, tracking steep losses among Asian peers amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of the global AI investment boom.
Technoprobe, Siltronic and Soitec each fell more than 4%, while ASM International, BE Semiconductor, Aixtron, STMicroelectronics and Infineon all dropped more than 3% by 07:34 GMT.
The declines followed a sharp selloff in South Korean memory giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which closed 3% and 4.2% lower, respectively. The benchmark Kospi index fell 3.7% to 5,552.74, snapping two consecutive sessions of gains and marking its lowest closing level since April 7.
The rebound in Asian chip stocks over the past two sessions proved short-lived, as lingering concerns over credit and profitability tied to AI-related investment remained unresolved.
The Tuesday selloff comes after shares tied to AI rebounded on Wall Street on Monday, clawing back part of last week's steep losses, while the rest of the market stayed shaky.
The S&P 500 climbed 0.4%, bouncing off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.1% on the strength of its heavy tech weighting. Most U.S. stocks outside the AI and technology sectors fell, however.
European markets fared worse, with major indexes sliding more than 1% after violent protests raised the prospect that France's government may need to boost spending to quell voter anger. That, in turn, added pressure to bond markets, pushing yields higher around the world.

Shares of car manufacturer General Motors sank premarket on a disappointing adjusted earnings per share forecast, while 3M gained after the Scotch Tape-maker expanded its commercial relationship with e-commerce titan Amazon.
Elon Musk's SpaceX and streaming giant Netflix are among the headliners in post-market results.
Elsewhere, oil prices climbed, with benchmark Brent crude futures up 1.3% to $110.92 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures climbed 1.5% to $100.02 a barrel.
Brent settled within touching distance of a five-month high on Monday, even though it had fallen earlier in the session on reports that the U.S. and Iran may have reached a breakthrough in mediated negotiations.
However, that decline had a short shelf life. Oil prices surged once again after Iran's First Vice President said the country had "no choice but to exercise sovereignty" over the Strait of Hormuz, exacerbating worries over crude supply disruptions in the critical chokepoint.
"[T]hat added to the sense that a deal before the U.S. midterms in two weeks' time is going to be challenging, while investors are also concerned that the U.S. administration may be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms as Iran's increased strikes in Hormuz have now slowed the increase in oil flows through Hormuz that had emerged over the previous couple of months," analysts at Deutsche Bank said in a note.
Recent strikes on vessels near Hormuz have slowed the flow of oil through the waterway. Hormuz has been largely shuttered since after the start of a joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran in late February, although reported shipping figures have indicated that supplies have shown signs of recovery.
